## One equation, two forces {#sec-equation}

Almost no physiological variable stays still, and almost none wanders off
without bound: it fluctuates around an equilibrium that something pulls it
back to. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process [@uhlenbeck1930] is the simplest
mathematical form of that idea:

$$
\mathrm{d}X_t \;=\; \theta\,(\mu - X_t)\,\mathrm{d}t \;+\; \sigma\,\mathrm{d}W_t .
$$ {#eq-ou}

The first term is the **drift**: a restoring force that pushes $X_t$
towards $\mu$ with a strength proportional to the distance. The second is
the **diffusion**: the increments of a Brownian motion $W_t$, which perturb
it relentlessly. The parameter $\theta > 0$ has units of frequency, and its
inverse $1/\theta$ is the time constant with which the system forgets a
perturbation.

## Exact solution {#sec-solution}

Unlike most stochastic differential equations, @eq-ou can be solved in
closed form [@sarkka2019].

::: {#prp-solution}
## Transition distribution

For $t \ge 0$ and initial condition $X_0 = x_0$,

$$
X_t \mid X_0 = x_0 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(
\mu + (x_0 - \mu)\,e^{-\theta t},\;\;
\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\bigl(1 - e^{-2\theta t}\bigr)
\right).
$$ {#eq-transition}
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $Y_t = e^{\theta t}(X_t - \mu)$. By Itô's formula,
$\mathrm{d}Y_t = \theta e^{\theta t}(X_t - \mu)\,\mathrm{d}t + e^{\theta t}\,\mathrm{d}X_t = \sigma e^{\theta t}\,\mathrm{d}W_t$:
the drift cancels. Integrating and rearranging,

$$
X_t = \mu + (x_0 - \mu)\,e^{-\theta t} + \sigma\int_0^t e^{-\theta (t - s)}\,\mathrm{d}W_s .
$$

The stochastic integral of a deterministic integrand is Gaussian with mean
zero and, by the Itô isometry, its variance is
$\sigma^2\int_0^t e^{-2\theta(t-s)}\,\mathrm{d}s = \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}(1 - e^{-2\theta t})$.
:::

Two immediate consequences. As $t \to \infty$ the process forgets where it
started and reaches the stationary distribution
$\mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu,\, \sigma^2/2\theta\bigr)$. And in that regime the
autocovariance decays exponentially,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h}) \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\,e^{-\theta |h|},
$$ {#eq-autocov}

which is exactly what "noise with memory" means.

## Simulation {#sec-simulation}

@eq-transition gives an **exact** simulation scheme for any step $\Delta$:
just sample the Gaussian transition. The generic alternative, valid for any
equation, is the Euler–Maruyama scheme [@kloeden1992], which replaces
differentials by finite increments.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ou_exact <- function(n, dt, theta, mu, sigma, x0) {
  a <- exp(-theta * dt)
  s <- sigma * sqrt((1 - a^2) / (2 * theta))
  x <- numeric(n + 1)
  x[1] <- x0
  z <- rnorm(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x[i + 1] <- mu + (x[i] - mu) * a + s * z[i]
  x
}

ou_euler <- function(n, dt, theta, mu, sigma, x0) {
  x <- numeric(n + 1)
  x[1] <- x0
  z <- rnorm(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    x[i + 1] <- x[i] + theta * (mu - x[i]) * dt + sigma * sqrt(dt) * z[i]
  }
  x
}
```
:::


@fig-paths shows twelve paths starting far from equilibrium, together with
the mean and the $\pm 2$ standard deviation band predicted by
@eq-transition.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1930)
theta <- 1; mu <- 0; sigma <- 1; x0 <- 4
dt <- 0.02
tt <- seq(0, 8, by = dt)

paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:12, function(k) {
  data.frame(t = tt, k = k,
             x = ou_exact(length(tt) - 1, dt, theta, mu, sigma, x0))
}))
theory <- data.frame(
  t = tt,
  m = mu + (x0 - mu) * exp(-theta * tt),
  s = sqrt(sigma^2 / (2 * theta) * (1 - exp(-2 * theta * tt)))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(t, ymin = m - 2 * s, ymax = m + 2 * s), theory,
              fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.22) +
  geom_line(aes(t, x, group = k), paths, linewidth = 0.25, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(aes(t, x), subset(paths, k == 1), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(t, m), theory, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = expression("Time (in units of " * 1 / theta * ")"),
       y = expression(X[t]))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Twelve paths with $\theta = 1$, $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$ and initial condition $x_0 = 4$. Dashed line: theoretical mean. Band: ±2 theoretical standard deviations.](index_files/figure-html/fig-paths-1.svg){#fig-paths fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


## The Euler–Maruyama bias {#sec-euler}

Does it matter which scheme we use? Euler–Maruyama applied to @eq-ou is an
autoregressive process with coefficient $1 - \theta\Delta$ and innovation
variance $\sigma^2\Delta$, whose stationary variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{EM}} \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2\Delta}{1 - (1 - \theta\Delta)^2}
\;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\cdot\frac{2}{2 - \theta\Delta}.
$$ {#eq-bias}

The scheme **inflates the variance** by a factor $2/(2 - \theta\Delta)$,
and becomes unstable when $\theta\Delta \ge 2$. We check this by simulating
long series with both schemes.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
steps <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 1.5)
n <- 2e5

bias <- do.call(rbind, lapply(steps, function(h) {
  data.frame(
    h = h,
    scheme = c("Euler–Maruyama", "Exact"),
    ratio = c(var(ou_euler(n, h, 1, 0, 1, 0)),
              var(ou_exact(n, h, 1, 0, 1, 0))) / 0.5   # exact: 1 / (2 · 1)
  )
}))

ggplot(bias, aes(h, ratio)) +
  geom_function(fun = function(h) 2 / (2 - h), colour = "grey45") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = scheme), size = 2.2, fill = "white") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Euler–Maruyama" = 16, "Exact" = 21)) +
  labs(x = expression(theta * Delta),
       y = "Simulated variance / exact variance")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Simulated stationary variance, relative to the exact one, as a function of the dimensionless step $\theta\Delta$. Filled circles: Euler–Maruyama. Open circles: exact scheme. Line: prediction of the bias equation.](index_files/figure-html/fig-bias-1.svg){#fig-bias fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


With $\theta\Delta = 0.1$ the excess is already 5%. The rule of thumb: if
the equation is linear, always use the exact transition; if it is not,
choose $\Delta$ at least an order of magnitude below the fastest time
constant in the system.

## Estimating the parameters {#sec-estimation}

Observed at regular intervals $\Delta$, an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process is
exactly an AR(1):

$$
X_{k+1} = a + b\,X_k + e_k, \qquad
b = e^{-\theta\Delta},\quad a = \mu\,(1 - b),\quad
\operatorname{Var}(e_k) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\,(1 - b^2).
$$ {#eq-ar1}

Conditional maximum likelihood therefore reduces to a linear regression of
each observation on the previous one, followed by inverting @eq-ar1.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_ou <- function(x, dt) {
  x0 <- x[-length(x)]
  x1 <- x[-1]
  b <- cov(x0, x1) / var(x0)
  a <- mean(x1) - b * mean(x0)
  s2 <- mean((x1 - a - b * x0)^2)
  theta <- -log(b) / dt
  c(theta = theta, mu = a / (1 - b), sigma = sqrt(2 * theta * s2 / (1 - b^2)))
}
```
:::


As a toy example, think of an RR interval fluctuating around 850 ms with a
time constant of 5 s, recorded once per second for ten minutes.


::: {#tbl-fit .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='True and estimated parameters from a single ten-minute series.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1930)
truth <- c(theta = 0.2, mu = 850, sigma = 20)
x <- ou_exact(600, 1, truth[["theta"]], truth[["mu"]], truth[["sigma"]], 850)

estimate <- fit_ou(x, dt = 1)
tab <- rbind(Truth = truth, Estimate = estimate)
colnames(tab) <- c("$\\theta$ (1/s)", "$\\mu$ (ms)",
                   "$\\sigma$ (ms/$\\sqrt{\\text{s}}$)")
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|         | $\theta$ (1/s)| $\mu$ (ms)| $\sigma$ (ms/$\sqrt{\text{s}}$)|
|:--------|--------------:|----------:|-------------------------------:|
|Truth    |          0.200|     850.00|                          20.000|
|Estimate |          0.217|     848.64|                          20.149|


:::
:::


## The hard parameter {#sec-hard}

The previous example had a series of 120 time constants on its side. With
short recordings the story changes, because information about $\theta$
does not depend on the number of observations but on **how many times the
process managed to return to its mean**. We check this by repeating the fit
over thousands of series of two durations, with the same step
$\Delta = 0.1/\theta$.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1930)
estimate_theta <- function(n, dt = 0.1) {
  x <- ou_exact(n, dt, 1, 0, 1, rnorm(1, 0, sqrt(0.5)))
  fit_ou(x, dt)[["theta"]]
}

mc <- rbind(
  data.frame(series = "short", theta = replicate(3000, estimate_theta(100))),
  data.frame(series = "long", theta = replicate(3000, estimate_theta(1000)))
)

ggplot(mc, aes(theta, linetype = series)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0.55, bw = "SJ", key_glyph = "path") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(short = "dashed", long = "solid"),
    breaks = c("short", "long"),
    labels = expression(T == 10 / theta, T == 100 / theta)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(theta) / theta), y = "Density")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Sampling distribution of the estimator of $\theta$, relative to the true value, for series lasting 10 and 100 time constants. The dotted line marks the unbiased value.](index_files/figure-html/fig-theta-1.svg){#fig-theta fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::




With ten time constants, the estimator overestimates $\theta$ by
47% on average and its standard
deviation is 0.67: the data barely pin down its order of
magnitude. With a hundred, the bias falls to
4% and the spread to
0.16. Sampling faster does not help; recording for longer
does.

## A physiological reading {#sec-reading}

The stationary variance $\sigma^2/2\theta$ mixes two different things: how
much noise comes in ($\sigma$) and how strongly it is corrected ($\theta$).
A system with $\theta = 0.2$ and $\sigma = 20$ has exactly the same standard
deviation (31.6) as another with $\theta = 2$ and $\sigma = 63.2$, but the
second forgets ten times faster. An index of total variability cannot tell
them apart; the autocorrelation in @eq-autocov can. Separating *how much it
fluctuates* from *how fast it is regulated* is precisely what a dynamical
model adds to a descriptive statistic.

In the [next post](../inflammatory-reflex/index.qmd) we use this process as
one piece of a larger model: an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck vagal tone whose mean
$\mu$ is no longer constant, because the immune system moves it.
